outcome: Alive and independent (Oxford Handicap Score 0-2) at 6 months
population: Acute ischemic stroke patients within 6 hours of symptom onset

hypotheses.title: Moderate benefit of IV alteplase in middle-aged acute ischemic stroke patients (age 50-69)
hypotheses.hypothesis: Among acute ischemic stroke patients treated within 6 hours, those aged 50-69 who receive IV alteplase have a moderate increase in the probability of being alive and independent (Oxford Handicap Score 0-2) at 6 months compared with control.

subgroup.notes: Age recorded in years at baseline. This subgroup is a contiguous middle-age band; consider sensitivity to alternative nearby cutpoints (e.g., 50-64, 55-74) and treating age continuously with an interaction term.

rationale: Physiologic plausibility: Middle-aged patients (50-69) generally have fewer age-related microvascular changes and less frailty than older patients, preserving collateral circulation and increasing the likelihood that reperfusion salvages penumbral tissue while limiting hemorrhagic risk.

Comorbidity profile: Compared with older cohorts, this age band typically has a lower prevalence of pre-stroke disability and severe comorbidity (e.g., advanced heart failure, severe chronic kidney disease), which improves the chance that reperfusion translates into functional independence rather than survival with disability.

Trial evidence and subgroup signals: Pooled subgroup analyses from thrombolysis trials and registries often show consistent or numerically greater absolute functional benefit in non-elderly and middle-aged adults compared with the very old, supporting an expectation of at least a moderate benefit in this band.

Risk–benefit balance: Rates of symptomatic intracranial hemorrhage (sICH) and fatal bleeding rise with age; middle-aged patients have a lower baseline bleeding risk than the very elderly, making net clinical benefit more likely for the same relative reperfusion efficacy.

Clinical recovery potential: Younger brain plasticity and rehabilitation responsiveness in middle-aged adults increase the probability that reperfusion leads to a meaningful functional recovery at 6 months.
key_features: Age 50-69 (primary effect modifier)
Baseline stroke severity (NIHSS) — modifies absolute benefit
Time-to-treatment (onset-to-needle) — shorter times increase benefit
Pre-stroke functional status (baseline OHS/mRS) — lower baseline disability favors independence
Comorbidities that increase bleeding risk (anticoagulation, uncontrolled hypertension, prior stroke) — modify risk/benefit
confounders_and_bias_risks: Confounding by indication: clinicians may preferentially select patients for alteplase based on unmeasured clinical judgment correlated with age and prognosis (e.g., perceived penumbra on imaging), biasing subgroup effect estimates.

Baseline imbalance: age cohorts may differ systematically in NIHSS, pre-stroke OHS, time-to-treatment, imaging characteristics (ASPECTS), and vascular territory, which confound observed subgroup differences if not fully adjusted.

Selection bias and eligibility differences: IST-3 inclusion/exclusion criteria and site-level treatment practices could produce differences in which middle-aged patients were randomized/treated versus excluded, reducing generalizability.
Missing outcome and informative censoring: differential loss to follow-up or early post-randomization mortality could distort 6-month functional outcome comparisons (competing risks).
Multiple testing and subgroup discovery bias: small sample (n=200) and post-hoc subgrouping increase the probability of type I errors, exaggerated effect sizes (type M error), and unstable estimates.
Collider bias: conditioning on intermediate variables (e.g., survival to discharge, receiving rehabilitation) can induce spurious associations between treatment and outcome within the age subgroup.

analyses: Primary adjusted subgroup effect: estimate the absolute risk difference and risk ratio for OHS 0-2 at 6 months comparing alteplase vs control within age 50-69 using a doubly-robust estimator (AIPW or TMLE) adjusting for baseline NIHSS, onset-to-treatment time, pre-stroke OHS, sex, systolic BP, glucose, atrial fibrillation, and prior antiplatelet/anticoagulant use; report 95% CIs and bootstrap CIs given small sample.

Interaction test: fit a logistic regression (or Poisson binomial for risk ratios) in the full sample with terms for treatment, subgroup indicator (50-69 vs others), and treatment*subgroup interaction; report interaction coefficient, p-value, and absolute differences to test heterogeneity.

Balance assessment and propensity-adjusted estimate: within the 50-69 subgroup, examine baseline covariate balance by randomized arm; if imbalance exists, implement propensity score weighting or matching within the subgroup and estimate treatment effect (ATE) with robust SEs.

Sensitivity to continuous age modeling: model age continuously with a treatment*age interaction (including splines) to evaluate whether the effect is specific to the 50-69 band or reflects a continuous age trend.

Missing data and competing risks: perform multiple imputation for missing covariates/outcomes under MAR, and conduct sensitivity analyses for missing-not-at-random (e.g., worst/best case imputation). Consider Fine-Gray or cause-specific analyses if competing risks (death) are substantial.
Robustness and small-sample checks: bootstrap CIs, permutation tests for interaction, and leave-one-site-out analyses (if multi-center) to assess estimate stability.

Unmeasured confounding sensitivity: calculate E-values for observed effect estimates and perform Rosenbaum bounds (if using matched analyses) to quantify the strength of an unmeasured confounder needed to explain away the effect.
negative_controls: Outcome falsification: an outcome plausibly unrelated to alteplase (e.g., non-stroke-related elective hospital admissions in follow-up window) to test for residual bias; expect no treatment association.

Exposure falsification: a baseline variable that should not affect future treatment assignment (e.g., study site administrative ID if randomization was centralized) as a negative control for confounding checks.
robustness: Re-specify subgroup using adjacent cutpoints (50-64, 55-74) and compare effect estimates to assess sensitivity to the chosen band.
Stratify analyses by key modifiers: baseline NIHSS (mild/moderate/severe) and onset-to-treatment (<3 h vs 3-6 h) to detect effect modification within the age band.
Exclude patients with high baseline pre-stroke disability (OHS >1) to test whether benefit is confined to those with good baseline function.
Bayesian shrinkage: fit a hierarchical model to stabilize subgroup estimate and reduce overestimation from small sample size (report posterior credible intervals and prior sensitivity).

caveats: This hypothesis concerns effect modification, not a claim of causality specifically in the subgroup beyond what is supported by randomized comparisons; subgroup-specific randomized balance may be imperfect in small samples.

The IST-3 sample size indicated (n=200) is small for reliable interaction testing; non-significant interaction does not rule out clinically meaningful heterogeneity, and significant findings may be unstable and susceptible to type I error.

Dichotomizing age loses information and may produce arbitrary thresholds; findings should be corroborated with continuous-age interaction models and external datasets or meta-analytic pooling before changing practice.

Residual confounding is possible even in randomized trials when analyzing subgroups; unmeasured variables (imaging penumbra, infarct core size) that influence selection and prognosis may bias subgroup results.

Interpret subgroup effect in the context of overall trial results, prior randomized evidence and safety signals (sICH rates). Replication in larger samples or pooled individual patient data is required before recommending differential treatment by age alone.

hypotheses.title: Older patients (70-79) have reduced but still positive net benefit from IV alteplase at 6 months
hypotheses.hypothesis: Among acute ischemic stroke patients treated within 6 hours, those aged 70–79 years experience a smaller absolute benefit from IV alteplase (r-tPA) on the outcome Alive & independent (Oxford Handicap Score 0–2) at 6 months than younger patients, but the treatment effect remains positive compared with control.

subgroup.notes: Age should be coded in completed years at stroke onset. Subgroup excludes patients <70 and >=80. If only categorical age is available, use the trial's 70–79 bin. When possible also analyze age continuously and with splines to check the 70–79 threshold.

rationale: Increased bleeding risk and cerebral small vessel disease with aging: vascular fragility and accumulated microangiopathy increase the risk of symptomatic intracerebral hemorrhage (sICH) after thrombolysis, which reduces net clinical benefit in older adults.

Reduced recovery capacity and neuroplasticity: biologic ageing and higher frailty/comorbidity burden reduce functional recovery potential after reperfusion, yielding smaller absolute gains in functional independence even when recanalization is successful.

Higher competing risk of death and baseline disability: older patients tend to have higher baseline pre-stroke disability and non-stroke competing risks (cardiac events, infections), which attenuate the absolute benefit observed on 6‑month functional outcomes.

Empirical signals from RCTs and registries: pooled analyses and registry data have generally shown attenuated absolute benefit from thrombolysis with increasing age (but not consistent complete loss of benefit for the 70–79 decade), supporting the hypothesis that benefit is reduced yet may remain positive in this age band.
key_features: Age 70–79 (defined as completed years at onset)
Baseline stroke severity (NIHSS)
Pre-stroke function (pre-stroke OHS)
Onset-to-treatment time
Comorbidity burden (atrial fibrillation, diabetes, hypertension) and measures of frailty
confounders_and_bias_risks: Randomization imbalance within the 70–79 subgroup: although overall randomization preserves balance, covariate imbalance can occur by chance in subgroups and bias subgroup-specific estimates.

Confounding by baseline stroke severity and pre-stroke disability: older patients may have higher NIHSS or more pre-stroke limitation, which mediate or confound observed treatment differences if not properly adjusted.

Selection bias / healthy enrollee effect: trial inclusion may preferentially select fitter older patients (survivor bias), limiting generalizability and potentially underestimating harm in the general elderly population.

Differential missingness/informative censoring: older patients may have higher loss to follow-up or death before assessment, biasing functional outcome estimates if missingness is not handled appropriately.
Measurement error and outcome misclassification: OHS assessment subjectivity and inter-rater variability can disproportionately affect older patients with multimorbidity.
Collider bias if conditioning on post-randomization variables (e.g., restricting to survivors or those reperfused), which can distort subgroup effect estimates.

analyses: Primary: estimate absolute risk difference (ARR) and relative risk (RR) for OHS 0–2 at 6 months comparing alteplase vs control within the 70–79 group using intention-to-treat population. Use marginal standardization (G-computation) from a logistic regression adjusted for key baseline covariates (NIHSS, pre-stroke OHS, onset-to-treatment time, atrial fibrillation, diabetes, systolic BP, imaging ischemia) to obtain adjusted risks and ARRs with 95% CIs (bootstrap for CIs given small sample).

Interaction test: fit a model on the full sample with a treatment × indicator(age 70–79) interaction term (adjusted for the same covariates). Report the interaction coefficient, 95% CI, and p-value to formally test whether effect differs vs other ages.

Robust (doubly robust) estimation: estimate subgroup-specific treatment effects using IPTW or a doubly robust estimator (e.g., targeted maximum likelihood estimation or augmented-IPTW) to guard against model misspecification.

Continuous-age sensitivity: model age as a continuous variable with restricted cubic splines and include a treatment×age spline interaction to assess non-linearity and whether the 70–79 band corresponds to a gradual trend vs threshold effect; plot marginal treatment effect across age with CIs.

Safety/mediator check: compare rates of symptomatic intracerebral hemorrhage, early mortality (e.g., 30-day), and recanalization surrogates by treatment within the 70–79 group to examine mechanisms for reduced benefit.
Missing data and robustness: perform multiple imputation for missing covariates/outcomes and re-run primary analyses; perform per-protocol analyses excluding major protocol violators and cross-overs.
Unmeasured confounding sensitivity: compute E-values for observed ARRs to quantify how strong an unmeasured confounder would need to be to explain away the subgroup effect.
Uncertainty quantification: report exact subgroup sample size, event counts, and wide CIs; use bootstrap or permutation testing to account for small-sample distributional issues.
negative_controls: Test for association between treatment assignment and baseline variables measured before randomization (should be null) as a falsification check for analytic errors.
Falsification outcome unrelated to thrombolysis (e.g., incidence of non-neurologic elective procedures within 6 months) to check for residual bias in outcome ascertainment.
robustness: Repeat subgroup analysis using alternative age bins (e.g., 65–74, 75–84) and continuous-age interaction to assess sensitivity to bin choice.
Restrict analysis to onset-to-treatment ≤3 hours and separately to 3–6 hours to see whether time modifies the age-by-treatment relationship.
Restrict to patients without pre-stroke disability (pre-stroke OHS 0–1) to assess influence of baseline function.
Exclude patients with major protocol deviations or those with large vessel occlusion who subsequently received endovascular therapy (if present) to reduce treatment contamination.

caveats: Subgroup analyses are exploratory: even in an RCT, subgroup-specific estimates are less precise and susceptible to chance imbalances; absence of a significant interaction does not prove homogeneity, and a significant interaction can be chance without biological plausibility.

Scale matters: effect modification can differ on absolute vs relative scales. Older patients often have higher baseline risk so a smaller relative benefit can still translate into a meaningful absolute benefit (or vice versa). Present both ARR and RR.

Sample size and power limitations: with an overall sample of ~200 (and a smaller 70–79 subgroup), statistical power to detect realistic interaction effects will be low; expect wide CIs and emphasize estimation over dichotomous significance testing.
Generalizability: IST-3 enrollees may be a selected, fitter subset of older adults; results may not generalize to community or unselected elderly patients.

Causality vs association: while randomization supports causal inference overall, subgroup estimates can be confounded by post-randomization selection and chance imbalance. Interpret subgroup effects cautiously and in the context of mechanistic/safety data (e.g., sICH rates).

hypotheses.title: Younger-elderly (age 60-69) derive the greatest net benefit-to-risk from IV alteplase in acute ischemic stroke
hypotheses.hypothesis: Among acute ischemic stroke patients treated within 6 hours, those aged 60-69 have a larger net benefit (higher absolute increase in proportion alive and independent [OHS 0-2 at 6 months] minus harms such as symptomatic ICH) from IV alteplase compared with other age bands.

subgroup.notes: Age defined in years at stroke onset. Use integer years recorded at baseline; consider sensitivity using age as continuous with spline-based interaction to verify non-linearity. If age is missing, report extent and handle via multiple imputation.

rationale: Physiologic reserve and neural plasticity: Compared with older age bands (>70), patients aged 60-69 typically retain greater functional reserve and capacity for post-stroke recovery, which increases the probability that successful reperfusion translates into an independent outcome (OHS 0-2).

Lower absolute hemorrhage risk than older elderly: Risk of symptomatic intracerebral haemorrhage (sICH) after thrombolysis increases with age; patients in their 60s commonly have less cerebral small-vessel disease and vessel fragility than octogenarians, producing a more favorable harm profile for alteplase.

Sufficient baseline stroke burden and comorbidity balance: Compared with younger adults (<60) who often have different etiologies (e.g., cardioembolic or dissection), the 60-69 band frequently represents patients with modifiable large-vessel or small-vessel disease whose deficits are amenable to reperfusion — producing a higher absolute benefit when reperfusion succeeds.

Treatment-window applicability: In the 0–6 hour window studied (IST-3 context), time-dependent benefit of alteplase is preserved and the 60-69 group is less likely than the very elderly to have competing non-stroke mortality or severe pre-stroke disability that would blunt functional benefit.

Net-benefit balance (benefit minus harm): Because net benefit is driven by both the absolute increase in good outcomes and the absolute increase in major harms (e.g., sICH), the intermediate age band minimizes harms while preserving substantial recovery potential, yielding a higher net benefit-to-risk ratio.
key_features: Age 60-69 (feature defining subgroup)
Functional outcome at 6 months: OHS 0-2 (primary benefit metric)
Symptomatic intracerebral haemorrhage within 7–14 days (primary harm metric for net-benefit calculation)
Baseline stroke severity (NIHSS) — strong prognostic confounder
Onset-to-treatment time (minutes) — effect modifier of reperfusion benefit
confounders_and_bias_risks: Baseline stroke severity (NIHSS): if imbalanced across age bands, can mimic or mask age-treatment interaction.
Onset-to-treatment time: systematic differences in time-to-needle by age (e.g., delayed presentation in some ages) confound effect estimates.
Pre-stroke disability (pre-stroke mRS) and comorbidities (anticoagulant use, atrial fibrillation, diabetes, hypertension): influence both treatment effect and risk of haemorrhage.

Selection/eligibility and collider bias: clinicians may selectively enroll or treat patients within certain age bands (or exclude frail older patients), producing non-random differences within an RCT subgroup or in observational samples.
Center- or physician-level practice patterns (cluster effects): differential use of alteplase, CT/CTA selection, or post-stroke care across centers could confound subgroup comparisons.
Small sample / low subgroup counts (sample size = 200): limited events within the 60-69 subgroup will generate imprecise estimates and increase risk of Type I/II errors and exaggerated effect sizes.
Missing outcome or differential loss to follow-up by age could bias observed 6-month functional outcome rates.
Measurement/definition issues: dichotomizing OHS (0-2) reduces information and can distort subgroup comparisons if severity distributions differ by age.

analyses: Primary subgroup ITT estimate: calculate absolute risk difference and relative effect (risk ratio or odds ratio) for OHS 0-2 at 6 months in the 60-69 subgroup (treated vs control) along with 95% CI; report event counts and N in subgroup.

Interaction test: fit a logistic regression for OHS 0-2 including main effects (treatment, age-group indicator 60-69 vs others) and their interaction; adjust for prespecified covariates (baseline NIHSS, onset-to-treatment time, pre-stroke mRS, atrial fibrillation, diabetes, center fixed effects). Report interaction coefficient, 95% CI, and p-value.

Causal / doubly robust estimates: use propensity-score stratification or inverse probability weighting (IPW) combined with outcome regression (doubly robust estimator) to estimate subgroup-specific average treatment effect, adjusting for baseline covariates listed above — useful if any deviations from randomization occurred or for exploratory per-protocol analyses.

Net-benefit calculation: define net benefit = absolute increase in OHS 0-2 attributable to alteplase minus w*(absolute increase in sICH), where w is a harm weight (e.g., baseline approach: w = 1; then vary w in sensitivity analyses). Present absolute numbers (NNT for benefit and NNH for harm) and net benefit across plausible weights.

Continuous-age interaction and non-linearity: model age as continuous with restricted cubic splines and include a treatment-by-age spline interaction to identify the age range with maximal estimated treatment effect; plot marginal treatment effect by age with confidence bands.

Robustness and sensitivity checks: (a) repeat analyses excluding patients on therapeutic anticoagulation or with very high baseline NIHSS; (b) per-protocol/as-treated analysis to assess impact of crossovers; (c) multiple imputation for missing covariates/outcomes; (d) bootstrap resampling to obtain CIs for net-benefit metrics.

Multiplicity and stability: report raw subgroup p-values and perform a prespecified false-discovery control (e.g., limit the number of subgroup tests or report adjusted p-values). Also perform leave-one-center-out to test stability to influential centers.
negative_controls: Outcome unlikely to be affected by alteplase (e.g., hospitalization for fracture or non-stroke elective surgery within 6 months) to check for residual bias in outcome ascertainment.
An early non-neurologic adverse event with no plausible mechanistic link to alteplase (e.g., dermatologic outpatient visits) as a falsification outcome.
robustness: Alternative age bands and binning: test adjacent bands (55–64, 65–74) and broader categories to assess sensitivity to the 60–69 cutpoint.
Continuous-age specification: compare categorical vs continuous (spline) interaction results to confirm the observed peak in the 60s is not an artifact of binning.
Bayesian hierarchical modeling across age bands to borrow strength and obtain stabilized subgroup estimates with appropriate shrinkage.
E-value calculation for the observed subgroup treatment effect to quantify the minimum strength of an unmeasured confounder needed to explain away the association.

caveats: Subgroup findings are exploratory and, even in randomized trials, interaction tests have low power; a statistically significant overall treatment effect does not guarantee a reliable within-subgroup causal estimate and a null interaction does not prove homogeneity.

Net benefit depends on how harms and benefits are weighted. Different clinical stakeholders may choose different weights for sICH versus functional independence; report a range of weights rather than a single summary metric.

Small sample size (total N=200) and likely small N in the 60–69 subgroup will produce wide confidence intervals and unstable estimates — avoid strong clinical recommendations based on imprecise estimates.

Post-hoc subgroup selection and multiple testing inflate Type I error risk — prespecify subgroup analyses when possible and interpret any positive finding as hypothesis-generating unless replicated in larger datasets or meta-analyses.

Age is a surrogate for many correlates (frailty, cerebrovascular burden, comorbidity). Any observed effect modification by age may reflect these correlated factors rather than age per se; adjust for available proxies (pre-stroke mRS, comorbidity indices) and consider frailty metrics if available.
Outcome dichotomization (OHS 0-2) loses information; complementary ordinal analyses of mRS (shift analysis) are recommended to corroborate findings.

hypotheses.title: Moderate NIHSS (5-14) experience greatest absolute benefit from IV alteplase
hypotheses.hypothesis: Among acute ischemic stroke patients treated within 6 hours, those with baseline NIHSS 5–14 will have the largest absolute improvement in probability of being alive and independent (OHS 0–2) at 6 months when randomized to IV alteplase versus control, compared with other NIHSS ranges.

subgroup.notes: NIHSS measured at baseline prior to randomization. This subgroup represents 'moderate' stroke severity commonly used in trials; analyze both as a categorical cut (5-14) and with sensitivity analyses treating NIHSS continuously or in finer bins (e.g., 0-4, 5-9, 10-14, 15+).

rationale: Biologic plausibility: Moderate NIHSS (5–14) reflects patients with substantial ischemic penumbra but still meaningful salvageable brain tissue and less extensive core infarct than severe strokes, so reperfusion therapies are more likely to translate into clinically meaningful functional recovery.

Absolute vs relative effects: Patients with very mild deficits (NIHSS <5) have high baseline probability of independence, leaving limited room for absolute gain; very severe strokes (NIHSS >14) have low baseline recovery probability and elevated risk of symptomatic intracranial hemorrhage, so absolute benefit from thrombolysis is attenuated.

Existing evidence base: Meta-analyses and pooled trial reports have repeatedly observed the largest absolute differences in favorable outcome in the moderate-severity ranges (commonly reported around NIHSS 5–14), consistent with a U-shaped pattern of absolute benefit across severity.

Risk–benefit balance: In moderate strokes the net clinical benefit (improvement in functional outcome minus treatment-related ICH risk) is expected to be maximal because hemorrhagic complication rates are lower than in severe strokes while treatment can salvage meaningful function.

Clinical pragmatism: Stroke guidelines and many clinicians already prioritize reperfusion for moderate deficits because changes in disability magnitude in this group more often alter independence status (OHS 0–2) at follow-up.
key_features: Baseline NIHSS (severity category: 5-14)
Onset-to-treatment time (minutes/hours) — earlier increases benefit
Age (years) — modifies baseline risk and bleeding risk
Baseline imaging markers of early ischemia / infarct core (if available: ASPECTS, CT signs) or plain CT appearance
Anticoagulation/antiplatelet status and comorbidities (e.g., diabetes, prior stroke, atrial fibrillation) that influence both baseline outcome and hemorrhagic risk
confounders_and_bias_risks: Subgroup imbalances despite randomization: randomization protects overall treatment effect, but within the NIHSS 5–14 stratum baseline covariates (age, time-to-treatment, comorbidities, imaging markers) may be uneven and confound subgroup effect estimates.
Confounding by indication / post-randomization selection: excluding patients or analyzing per-protocol can induce bias if cross-over or treatment deviations differ by severity.

Measurement error / misclassification of NIHSS: NIHSS is a single pre-randomization snapshot; inter-rater variability or missing/erroneous scores can misclassify patients across the 5–14 boundary and bias effect estimates toward the null.

Collider bias: stratifying on NIHSS (which may be influenced by pre-stroke factors that also affect outcomes) can open colliders if those factors are affected by both treatment assignment and outcome.
Small sample and multiple testing: the available sample (n=200) limits precision for subgroup absolute differences; multiple subgroup / cut-point testing increases false positive risk.
Differential missingness/loss to follow-up: if outcome ascertainment at 6 months differs by treatment within NIHSS groups, estimates of absolute benefit can be biased.

analyses: Primary: Estimate absolute risk difference (ARR) in proportion alive and independent (OHS 0–2 at 6 months) between alteplase and control within NIHSS 5–14 using intention-to-treat. Report ARR, 95% CI, and NNT = 1/ARR.

Interaction test: Fit a logistic regression for 6-month OHS 0–2 with terms for treatment, NIHSS-group (5–14 vs other), and a treatment × NIHSS-group interaction. Report interaction coefficient on the risk difference scale (via marginal standardization/g-computation) and p-value. Present both odds ratio interaction and marginal risk difference interaction.

Adjusted effect: Repeat subgroup-specific ARR using multivariable adjustment (age, onset-to-treatment time, prior stroke, diabetes, atrial fibrillation, baseline CT early ischemic change/ASPECTS if available) and present adjusted marginal probabilities (use g-computation or inverse probability weighting).

Continuous modeling: Model NIHSS as continuous with restricted cubic splines and include treatment × spline interactions to examine non-linear treatment effect heterogeneity across the NIHSS spectrum; visualize predicted probability of OHS 0–2 by baseline NIHSS for treated vs control with 95% CIs.

Robust estimation and inference for small samples: Use bootstrap (clustered on treatment arm if needed) to obtain CIs for subgroup ARRs and interaction contrasts; consider Firth's penalized logistic regression if separation occurs.
Safety trade-off: Within NIHSS 5–14 estimate treatment effect on symptomatic ICH and on mortality to quantify net clinical benefit (e.g., composite of OHS 0–2 minus sICH).
negative_controls: Test for treatment effect on pre-randomization baseline variables (should be null) to detect analytic pipeline errors.

If available, use an outcome unlikely to be affected by alteplase (e.g., non-stroke-related hospitalization or an adjudicated non-neurologic event) as a falsification endpoint; absence of effect increases confidence in specificity of detected subgroup effect.
Permutation test of the treatment × subgroup interaction (randomly permute treatment labels) to assess whether observed interaction is larger than expected by chance given small sample.
robustness: Sensitivity to cut-point: repeat analyses using alternative NIHSS bins (e.g., 0–4, 5–9, 10–14, 15+) and test for trend across ordered categories to ensure signal is not an artifact of the chosen 5–14 boundary.
Missing outcome sensitivity: perform multiple imputation for missing 6-month OHS under MAR, and worst-case / best-case imputation to bound ARR estimates.
Per-protocol and as-treated analyses: report but interpret cautiously; check whether cross-over or dose deviations modify subgroup findings.
Adjustment set variation: compare unadjusted, minimally adjusted (age, time-to-treatment), and fully adjusted models (add comorbidities, imaging markers) to evaluate stability of subgroup ARR.

caveats: Exploratory subgroup analysis: subgroup findings are hypothesis-generating and not definitive evidence for treatment restriction or universal application — interaction tests are often underpowered and multiple comparisons inflate false positive risk.

Scale dependence: effect modification can differ by scale (absolute risk difference vs relative risk/odds ratio). The hypothesis concerns absolute benefit; an apparent larger absolute benefit in 5–14 could coexist with similar relative risk across severities.

Generalizability: IST-3 population and the 6-hour treatment window include older and later-treated patients compared with other alteplase trials; results may not generalize to other settings or narrower time windows.

Causal inference limits: although the parent study is randomized, subgroup comparisons can be confounded by imbalances within strata and do not automatically imply individual-level treatment effect predictability.

Imprecision: with sample size ~200, confidence intervals for subgroup ARRs will be wide; absence of a statistically significant interaction does not rule out clinically important heterogeneity, and apparent subgroup differences may be due to chance.

hypotheses.title: Mild baseline NIHSS (≤4) have limited absolute benefit from IV alteplase
hypotheses.hypothesis: Among acute ischemic stroke patients treated (or randomized) within 6 hours, those with baseline NIHSS ≤ 4 (mild stroke) will experience a smaller absolute increase in the probability of being alive and independent (OHS 0–2) at 6 months with IV alteplase compared with control; the absolute benefit may be minimal and in some patients the risk (notably symptomatic intracranial hemorrhage) could offset benefit.

subgroup.notes: NIHSS is baseline (pre-randomization) score. Alternative encodings to check: NIHSS as continuous, cutpoints at ≤3 and ≤5, and spline modeling. Ensure NIHSS recorded before treatment decision. In IST-3 population consider potential enrichment for older patients and extended time window (up to 6 h).

rationale: High baseline good outcome probability: Patients with very mild deficits (NIHSS ≤ 4) have a high spontaneous recovery rate and therefore a high baseline probability of OHS 0–2 at 6 months; this reduces the possible absolute risk difference that thrombolysis can produce (ceiling effect).

Bleeding risk is fixed and absolute harm can outweigh small gains: The absolute risk of symptomatic intracerebral hemorrhage (sICH) after alteplase is non-zero; when the expected absolute benefit in good outcome is small, even a small absolute increase in sICH (with associated morbidity/mortality) may negate net clinical benefit.

Heterogeneity by mechanism and occlusion status: Mild deficits often reflect small lacunar syndromes or transient ischemia without a proximal large-vessel occlusion; thrombolysis is more likely to benefit patients with occlusive large-vessel thrombi. Without an occlusion, the biological plausibility of large benefit from thrombolysis is lower.

Observational and trial signals: Prior trials and registries have reported small absolute benefit from thrombolysis in minor strokes and ongoing clinical debate about net benefit in this subgroup, supporting testing of limited absolute effect in IST-3 data.

Measurement and timing issues: Mild deficits are more sensitive to variability in NIHSS measurement and early spontaneous improvement; small measurement or timing differences can shrink apparent treatment effects in the mild group.
key_features: Baseline NIHSS score ≤ 4 (mild stroke)
High baseline probability of good outcome (OHS 0–2) without intervention
Risk of symptomatic intracranial hemorrhage (sICH) after alteplase
Presence/absence of proximal large-vessel occlusion (if available from imaging)
Time-to-treatment (earlier treatment tends to increase absolute benefit)
confounders_and_bias_risks: Randomization not stratified by post-hoc subgroup: although IST-3 is randomized, subgroup comparisons are subject to chance baseline imbalances (age, pre-stroke mRS, comorbidities) that can bias subgroup effect estimates.
Measurement error/misclassification of NIHSS: small absolute differences in NIHSS scoring can move patients across the ≤4 threshold and change subgroup composition.

Unmeasured prognostic variables (e.g., presence of proximal occlusion on imaging, collateral status) that both modify treatment effect and correlate with NIHSS could confound interpretation if not adjusted for.

Selection or enrollment bias: patients with mild symptoms may have been selectively included/excluded (physician decision) or have different consent rates, creating non-random sampling of mild patients despite trial design.

Outcome assessment bias or missingness: mRS at 6 months may be missing or assessed non-blinded for some patients, and differential loss-to-follow-up between arms in mild subgroup could bias absolute estimates.
Multiplicity and data-driven subgroup selection (HypoGeniC): exploratory searching increases false-discovery risk; observed subgroup effects may be spurious.

analyses: Primary estimate: compute marginal absolute risk difference (ARD) for OHS 0–2 at 6 months comparing alteplase vs control within NIHSS ≤ 4 using covariate-adjusted g-computation (logistic regression + standardization) adjusted for pre-specified baseline covariates: age, sex, pre-stroke mRS, time-to-treatment, atrial fibrillation, diabetes, prior stroke, baseline glucose, and imaging center.

Interaction test: fit a model on the full sample with treatment × (NIHSS ≤ 4) interaction term to estimate the interaction on both absolute (identity-link linear model or g-computation derived marginal differences) and relative scales (log-binomial or Poisson with robust SEs); report interaction coefficient, 95% CI and p-value.

Continuous effect modification: model treatment × NIHSS as a continuous interaction (linear and restricted cubic spline) to assess monotonicity and to avoid artefacts of dichotomization; plot predicted absolute treatment effect across NIHSS values with bootstrap CIs.

Harm outcome: estimate absolute and relative differences in symptomatic intracerebral hemorrhage (sICH) and 6-month mortality within the NIHSS ≤ 4 subgroup and compute net clinical benefit measures (e.g., difference in OHS 0–2 minus weighting for sICH/mortality), with bootstrap CIs.

Robustness to confounding: perform inverse probability weighting (IPW) or doubly robust targeted maximum likelihood estimation (TMLE) adjusted for the same covariates; compare adjusted vs unadjusted estimates.

Sensitivity and subgroup checks: (a) repeat analysis in alternative cutpoints (≤3, ≤5); (b) stratify by time-to-treatment (<3h vs 3–6h), age (<80 vs ≥80), and imaging-occlusion status if available; (c) per-protocol analysis excluding major protocol deviations.
Uncertainty quantification for small sample: compute bootstrap (clustered by center if applicable) 95% CIs for ARD and interaction estimates; report number-needed-to-treat (NNT) with CIs.
Multiplicity and false discovery control: use permutation-based tests or adjust for multiple subgroup tests (e.g., Holm/Benjamini-Hochberg) and report which findings remain robust.

Falsification/E-value: compute E-value for observed ARD to quantify how strong an unmeasured confounder would need to be to explain away the effect; perform a negative-control outcome test if plausible (see below).
negative_controls: Negative-control outcome: an outcome not plausibly affected by alteplase (e.g., non-stroke-related hospitalization at 6 months) to check for spurious associations or differential measurement.
Negative-control subgroup: test interaction with a baseline variable not expected to modify effect (e.g., calendar month of enrollment) to assess risk of overfitting / multiplicity artifacts.
robustness: Alternate NIHSS encodings: dichotomize at multiple nearby cutpoints and model as continuous/spline to verify stability of the effect.
Exclude patients with baseline pre-stroke mRS > 1, or with major protocol deviations, to assess influence of frail/high-baseline-disability patients.
Adjust for center or include random intercept for recruiting center to account for center-level practice differences.
Examine influence of missing outcome data: perform multiple imputation under different missing-not-at-random scenarios and report how ARD varies.

caveats: Exploratory subgroup finding, not definitive: post-hoc or data-driven subgroup detection (HypoGeniC) can produce spurious interactions; these results should be considered hypothesis-generating and require replication in independent datasets or meta-analysis.

Limited sample size and power: with ~200 patients (and likely fewer in NIHSS ≤ 4), precision around absolute differences and interaction estimates will be poor; non-significant interaction does not rule out clinically important heterogeneity, and significant findings may be overestimated.

RCT design reduces confounding but does not immunize against subgroup imbalance: despite randomization, subgroup-specific baseline imbalances or measurement error can bias subgroup estimates if not properly adjusted.

Outcome definitions and weighing harms: a small absolute increase in OHS 0–2 must be interpreted alongside harms (sICH, death). Net clinical benefit requires integrated consideration of both benefit and harm and patient values.

Generalizability: IST-3 enrolled an older, broader time-window population (up to 6 hours) compared with contemporary practice; results for mild strokes in IST-3 may not generalize to populations with different imaging selection (e.g., routine vessel imaging) or earlier treatment windows.

Dichotomization limitations: threshold-based subgrouping (NIHSS ≤ 4) is pragmatic but arbitrary; clinical decisions should consider continuous stroke severity, imaging findings, and individualized risk–benefit assessment rather than an absolute cutpoint alone.

hypotheses.title: Severe baseline NIHSS (>=15) predicts lower absolute benefit of IV alteplase for 6-month independence
hypotheses.hypothesis: Among acute ischemic stroke patients treated within 6 hours, those with severe baseline neurological deficits (NIHSS >= 15) will have a lower probability of being alive and independent (Oxford Handicap Score 0-2) at 6 months and will experience a smaller absolute benefit from IV alteplase compared with patients with NIHSS < 15; severe patients will also have a higher rate of symptomatic intracerebral hemorrhage (sICH), which may limit net clinical benefit.

subgroup.notes: NIHSS measured at baseline prior to treatment. Threshold 15 is commonly used in stroke literature to define severe deficits; consider sensitivity to alternate cutpoints (e.g., 10, 20) and modeling NIHSS continuously or with splines.

rationale: Larger infarct territory and less salvageable penumbra: Higher NIHSS correlates with larger baseline infarct volume and more extensive ischemic injury; reperfusion with alteplase may be less likely to translate into functional independence because irreversible damage has already occurred.

Lower absolute benefit despite possible similar relative effect: Trial and observational summaries show relative benefit of thrombolysis can be present across severities but absolute risk difference in favorable outcome declines as baseline probability of a good outcome falls with increasing NIHSS (ceiling/floor effects).

Increased risk of hemorrhagic transformation: Severe strokes are associated with greater blood–brain barrier disruption and larger ischemic cores, which are established risk factors for symptomatic ICH after thrombolysis, reducing net benefit.

Differential mechanism of treatment failure: Severe deficits are more often due to proximal large-vessel occlusion (LVO). IV alteplase alone has lower recanalization rates for LVO compared with endovascular therapy, so alteplase's ability to salvage tissue in severe strokes may be limited in centers without EVT or prior to EVT availability.

Clinical trial subgroup findings and meta-analyses: Prior randomized-trial subgroup analyses and pooled data indicate that baseline NIHSS is a strong predictor of outcome and modifies absolute benefit/harm trade-offs for reperfusion therapies, supporting a priori expectation of smaller absolute gains in very severe strokes.
key_features: Baseline NIHSS (continuous and dichotomous at >=15)
Onset-to-treatment time (minutes/hours)
Imaging markers: baseline infarct size/ASPECTS, presence/location of large-vessel occlusion
Age and pre-stroke functional status (mRS), which interact with prognosis and absolute benefit
Coagulopathy/antiplatelet use, baseline glucose and blood pressure (predictors of sICH)
confounders_and_bias_risks: Confounding by indication and post-randomization selection: although IST-3 was randomized, subgroup analyses can show imbalance in baseline covariates by chance; in observational settings treatment decisions and exclusions (e.g., for EVT) can confound associations.
Collider bias from conditioning on post-randomization events (e.g., excluding patients who underwent EVT) or on variables affected by treatment.
Measurement error or inter-rater variability in NIHSS scoring leading to misclassification across the 15-point threshold.
Small subgroup sample (total n=200): limited power to detect interaction and imprecise estimates; estimates may be unstable and sensitive to a few outcomes.
Informative missingness or loss to follow-up on 6-month OHS (differential by severity or treatment) can bias effect estimates.
Changes in contemporaneous care (availability of EVT, supportive care differences) limit transportability of subgroup effects estimated in IST-3 era to current practice.

analyses: Primary: Intention-to-treat estimate of absolute risk difference (and risk ratio) for OHS 0-2 at 6 months comparing alteplase vs control separately within NIHSS >=15 and NIHSS <15 groups; report bootstrap 95% CIs.

Interaction test: fit a logistic regression for OHS 0-2 with terms for treatment, subgroup (NIHSS>=15), and their interaction; report the interaction coefficient, p-value, and confidence interval for the risk-difference scale (use marginal standardization to convert model outputs to absolute differences).

Continuous modifier analysis: model baseline NIHSS as continuous (restricted cubic splines, e.g., 3-5 knots) and include treatment × spline terms to estimate treatment effect as a function of NIHSS; plot predicted absolute benefit versus NIHSS with confidence bands.

Adjustments: repeat primary and interaction analyses adjusted for pre-specified prognostic covariates (age, onset-to-treatment time, baseline mRS, glucose, SBP, imaging ASPECTS or infarct size if available) to account for residual imbalance; use doubly robust estimator (IPTW + outcome regression) where appropriate.

Harm and net-benefit: estimate sICH rates and all-cause mortality within subgroups; compute absolute increase in sICH and combine with benefit to produce simple net-clinical-benefit metrics (e.g., NNT for independence vs NNH for sICH) and sensitivity analyses using alternative harm weights.

Sensitivity checks: (a) exclude patients who underwent EVT or analyze them separately; (b) vary NIHSS threshold (e.g., 10, 20) and test consistency; (c) per-protocol analyses excluding major protocol violations; (d) multiple imputation for missing outcomes and compare to complete-case results.
Stability and shrinkage: use hierarchical (Bayesian or penalized) subgroup models or empirical Bayes shrinkage to avoid overinterpretation of extreme subgroup estimates in small samples.
negative_controls: Test for interaction between treatment and a baseline variable not plausibly linked to alteplase effect (e.g., day of week of admission) as a falsification check.
Evaluate an outcome unlikely to be affected by thrombolysis (e.g., non-neurological infection within 7 days) for spurious subgroup differences.
robustness: Bootstrap CIs for subgroup estimates to reflect small-sample uncertainty.

E-value computation or tipping-point analysis to quantify strength of unmeasured confounding required to negate observed subgroup differences (relevant primarily if performing observational analyses).

Multiplicity-aware interpretation: report number of subgroup tests and avoid dichotomous claims based on nominal p-values; consider presenting posterior probabilities of clinically meaningful benefit under weakly informative priors.

caveats: Subgroup tests are inherently lower-powered and prone to false positives/negatives; a non-significant interaction does not prove absence of effect modification and a nominally significant interaction may be due to chance, particularly with n=200.
Threshold choice (NIHSS >=15) is somewhat arbitrary; continuous modeling is preferable to dichotomization where feasible and should be presented alongside the binary split.
Even in randomized data, subgroup analyses can suffer baseline imbalances by chance and should be interpreted in the context of adjusted and unadjusted estimates and robustness checks.

Net clinical benefit depends on how harms are weighted relative to functional independence; different stakeholders (patients, clinicians) may assign different weights to sICH vs disability, so any net-benefit metric should be presented under several plausible weighting schemes.

Generalisability: IST-3-era care patterns (limited access to EVT, different imaging selection) may differ from contemporary practice where endovascular therapy is widely available for LVOs; effect modification by NIHSS may be altered in current care settings.

Causality: interaction associations do not establish mechanistic causality without corroborating evidence (imaging, recanalization rates); interpret subgroup differences as hypothesis-generating if not pre-specified and/or underpowered.

hypotheses.title: Very high body weight (>=100 kg) reduces benefit of IV alteplase (effect modification by weight)
hypotheses.hypothesis: Among acute ischemic stroke patients randomized within 6 hours, patients with body weight >= 100 kg will experience less benefit from IV alteplase (recombinant tPA) on the probability of being alive and independent (OHS 0-2) at 6 months compared with lighter patients, because dose-capping at the absolute maximum dose produces lower mg/kg exposure and may reduce thrombolytic efficacy.

subgroup.notes: Weight in kilograms measured at baseline (pre-randomization). Encoding: use measured weight; if only categorical or BSA/BMI available, derive consistent bins. Note that alteplase dosing is typically 0.9 mg/kg up to an absolute maximum (commonly 90 mg), so patients >=100 kg are likely to receive a capped dose (<0.9 mg/kg). Consider rounding rules applied in IST-3 for dose calculation and identify patients with explicit dose-cap flag.

rationale: Pharmacologic dosing rule: Alteplase is dosed at 0.9 mg/kg with an absolute maximum total dose (commonly 90 mg). Patients weighing >=100 kg exceed the weight at which the 0.9 mg/kg rule reaches the cap (0.9*100 = 90 mg), so heavier patients will typically receive less than 0.9 mg/kg, leading to lower systemic mg/kg exposure.

Biologic plausibility: Lower per-kilogram exposure of tPA may reduce clot lysis probability and vessel recanalization rates, which are mechanistically linked to improved functional outcomes after ischemic stroke. Thus dose under-exposure in very heavy patients plausibly decreases treatment efficacy.

Obesity-related pathophysiology and comorbidity: Very high body weight is associated with pro-thrombotic states, endothelial dysfunction, and higher prevalence of comorbidities (diabetes, hypertension, OSA) that may both increase stroke severity and blunt recovery; these factors could interact with reduced drug exposure to yield lower net benefit.

Empirical signals from prior analyses: Although direct randomized evidence is limited, observational and subgroup reports have suggested altered outcomes or different safety/efficacy profiles in very heavy patients receiving weight-capped medications; this supports testing for treatment-by-weight interaction in IST-3 data.

Operational importance: If a true interaction exists, it has direct clinical implications (consider alternative dosing strategies, individualized dosing, or weight-specific counseling), making it a relevant hypothesis despite anticipated small subgroup sizes.
key_features: baseline body weight (kg)
actual alteplase total dose administered (mg)
calculated mg/kg dose received
dose-capped flag (yes/no) based on absolute max dose
baseline stroke severity (NIHSS), time-to-treatment
confounders_and_bias_risks: Residual confounding by baseline severity or stroke subtype: heavier patients may present with different baseline NIHSS or clot burden that independently affect outcome and interact with treatment response.

Differential randomization balance in small subgroup: with only ~200 patients total, the >=100 kg subgroup will be small and randomization may not be balanced across covariates within that subgroup, producing apparent effect modification.

Measurement error in weight or dose documentation: weight may be estimated rather than measured in emergency settings; dose administration records may be incomplete—misclassification of subgroup or mg/kg exposure will bias interaction estimates towards the null or unpredictably.

Post-randomization care and protocol deviations: heavier patients may receive different downstream care (imaging, endovascular therapy eligibility) or have more frequent dose adjustments/contraindications, creating collider or mediator bias if not addressed.

Selection/collider bias when conditioning on treated patients only: if analyses restricted to treated patients (per-protocol) rather than intention-to-treat, selection bias can distort subgroup effects.
Limited power and multiple testing: small sample size increases chance of type II error and unstable estimates; searching multiple cutpoints or subgroups inflates false-positive risk.

analyses: Primary test: fit an interaction model on the randomized sample: logistic regression for outcome (OHS 0-2 at 6 months) including terms for treatment (tPA vs control), subgroup indicator (weight >=100 kg), and treatment*subgroup interaction. Report interaction coefficient, p-value, and 95% CI; present adjusted and unadjusted models.

Estimate absolute treatment effect (risk difference) and relative effect (odds ratio or risk ratio) separately within weight <100 kg and >=100 kg strata. Report NNT where appropriate. Use intention-to-treat population for primary inference.

Continuous effect-modification analysis: model weight as a continuous variable with restricted cubic splines and include treatment*spline interactions to visualize how treatment effect varies continuously with weight; plot predicted absolute treatment benefit over weight with confidence bands.

Dose-exposure mediation check among treated: compute actual mg/kg received and a dose-capped indicator. In treated patients, test association between mg/kg (continuous) and outcome; perform mediation analysis to quantify how much of the weight-by-treatment interaction is explained by lower mg/kg exposure (e.g., causal mediation or g-computation), acknowledging assumptions.

Covariate-adjusted interaction: repeat interaction analysis adjusting for key prognostic covariates (age, baseline NIHSS, time from onset to randomization, pre-stroke mRS, atrial fibrillation, diabetes, hypertension) to reduce residual confounding and check stability of interaction estimate.

Robust causal estimators: apply doubly robust/AIPW or targeted maximum likelihood estimation (TMLE) to estimate subgroup-specific average treatment effects and interaction terms to improve bias-variance tradeoff in small samples.

Per-protocol and sensitivity analyses: (a) exclude patients with major protocol violations or missing dosing records; (b) perform complete-case and multiple-imputation analyses for missing outcome/covariate data.
Explore alternate thresholds and bins (e.g., 95 kg, 105 kg, BMI >=30/35) and report pre-specified threshold tests; correct for multiplicity or treat secondary thresholds as exploratory.
negative_controls: Test treatment*weight interaction on baseline, pre-randomization variables (e.g., baseline NIHSS or pre-stroke mRS); expectation: no interaction should be present — a non-null result indicates residual bias.

If available, test interaction on an outcome that cannot plausibly be affected by alteplase (e.g., pre-existing chronic conditions recorded at baseline or an outcome determined prior to randomization).
robustness: Assess the distribution of weights and the number/proportion of patients whose dose was capped; if few patients are actually capped, the hypothesized mechanism is less plausible.
E-value or quantitative bias analysis to assess how strong an unmeasured confounder would need to be to explain away an observed interaction.
Bootstrap CIs for interaction or subgroup effect estimates to reflect small-sample uncertainty.
Compare ITT vs per-protocol effects to evaluate sensitivity to protocol adherence and post-randomization selection.

caveats: Interaction tests are typically underpowered in small samples; absence of a statistically significant interaction does not exclude a clinically meaningful effect modification, and a statistically significant interaction in a small sample may be unstable.

Randomization ensures unbiased average treatment effect, but does not guarantee balance within small subgroups; adjusted analyses and robust estimators are essential but cannot fully substitute for adequate sample size.
If weight is estimated rather than directly measured, misclassification may bias results toward the null; ensure data quality checks and sensitivity to measurement method.

A detected weight-by-treatment interaction does not by itself prove dose-capping is the causal mechanism — other weight-associated factors (comorbidities, differing care patterns) could explain the finding. Mediation analysis can be suggestive but relies on strong assumptions.
Multiple testing and post-hoc selection of cutpoints inflate false discovery risk; pre-specify thresholds where possible and treat exploratory threshold searches as hypothesis-generating.

Generalizability: IST-3 population and dosing practices (absolute max dose used) may differ from other settings; any recommendation about changing dosing should rely on converging evidence (pharmacokinetic data, larger pooled analyses, or prospective studies) before clinical implementation.

hypotheses.title: Low body weight (<60 kg) modifies net benefit of IV alteplase—higher harm / lower probability of OHS 0-2 at 6 months
hypotheses.hypothesis: Among acute ischemic stroke patients treated with IV alteplase within 6 hours, patients with body weight < 60 kg have a lower probability of being alive and independent (Oxford Handicap Score 0–2) at 6 months compared with patients ≥ 60 kg, driven in part by a higher rate of symptomatic intracranial hemorrhage (sICH) and reduced physiologic reserve (frailty/malnutrition) that limits recovery.

subgroup.notes: Use measured baseline body weight (kg). If weight missing, use multiple imputation with predictors (age, sex, BMI if available, baseline NIHSS). Consider sex-specific distributions (absolute threshold may capture disproportionately more women). Sensitivity analyses using BMI (<20 kg/m2) and alternative thresholds (55, 65 kg).

rationale: Physiologic reserve and frailty: Low body mass often correlates with frailty and reduced nutritional reserve, which can impair recovery from ischemic brain injury and reduce tolerance to complications of therapy.

Bleeding susceptibility: Smaller body size may be associated with higher effective plasma concentration of fixed-dose alteplase and altered hemostatic balance, plausibly increasing risk of symptomatic intracranial hemorrhage (sICH) which strongly worsens functional outcome.

Dose-exposure and pharmacokinetics: Alteplase is given as fixed mg/kg in most protocols but dosing errors, rounding practices, or pharmacodynamic variability in low-weight patients could increase bleeding risk; even with weight-based dosing, low reserve may worsen consequences of hemorrhage.

Observed associations in related data: Prior observational and trial subgroup analyses have reported worse outcomes or higher complication rates in low-weight / low-BMI patients after acute interventions, supporting biological plausibility for effect modification.

Trade-off between reperfusion benefit and harm: For some subgroups (e.g., frail or low-weight), the absolute benefit from reperfusion may be smaller while absolute harm (sICH) is higher, shifting net benefit toward harm.
key_features: Baseline body weight (kg)
Symptomatic intracranial hemorrhage (sICH) within 7 days
Baseline stroke severity (NIHSS)
Age and frailty indicators (e.g., pre-stroke dependency, malnutrition markers)
Time-to-treatment (onset-to-needle)
confounders_and_bias_risks: Confounding by frailty/illness: Low weight may be a marker of chronic illness or frailty (unmeasured) that independently reduces recovery and increases bleeding risk—this could confound interpretation even in an RCT subgroup analysis.
Post-randomization collider bias: Conditioning on post-treatment variables (e.g., early neurological deterioration) could induce spurious associations between weight and outcome.
Measurement error and misclassification: Weight may be estimated or missing in acute settings; differential missingness by severity or treatment arm could bias results.
Small subgroup sample size and low power: With total N≈200, the low-weight subgroup may be small, producing imprecise estimates and unstable interaction tests (type I and II error concerns).
Sex confounding: Absolute weight threshold will capture more women; sex differences in outcome or treatment response could confound the apparent weight effect if not adjusted.

Dose and protocol adherence: If alteplase dosing or administration differs systematically by weight (rounding, errors), observed effect may reflect dosing differences rather than intrinsic susceptibility.

analyses: Primary interaction test: Fit an adjusted logistic regression for outcome (OHS 0–2 at 6 months) with terms for treatment (alteplase vs control), low_weight (<60 kg), and treatment*low_weight interaction. Adjust for baseline covariates: age, sex, baseline NIHSS, time-to-treatment, prior stroke, atrial fibrillation, diabetes, baseline glucose, baseline blood pressure, pre-stroke dependency, and study center (if applicable). Report interaction coefficient, p-value, and subgroup-specific adjusted absolute risk differences (marginal standardized risks) with 95% CIs.

Estimate subgroup-specific treatment effect: Use doubly robust/targeted maximum likelihood estimation (or propensity-score stratified/IPTW) to estimate the treatment effect (risk difference and risk ratio) separately in <60 kg vs ≥60 kg, with bootstrap CIs.

Bleeding mediation: Analyze sICH incidence by subgroup and treatment arm. Estimate the proportion of the subgroup treatment effect mediated by sICH using causal mediation analysis (natural direct/indirect effects), reporting assumptions and sensitivity to unmeasured mediator–outcome confounding.

Continuous modelling: Model weight continuously with restricted cubic splines and include a treatment*weight interaction to assess non-linear modification and identify empirical inflection points instead of relying solely on the 60 kg threshold.

Robustness/sensitivity checks: (a) repeat analyses using BMI (<20 kg/m2) and sex-specific weight thresholds; (b) alternative thresholds (55 and 65 kg); (c) restrict to patients with measured (not imputed) weight; (d) adjust for additional proxies of frailty (e.g., pre-stroke dependency, albumin if available); (e) multiple imputation for missing covariates and assessment of missingness mechanism.

Assess covariate balance: Within the low-weight subgroup, compare baseline characteristics across treatment arms to verify randomization balance; if imbalance exists, include imbalanced covariates in models or use adjusted estimators.

Quantify uncertainty and power: Report subgroup sample sizes, event counts (good outcome and sICH), and compute minimal detectable interaction effects given observed sample to contextualize negative/positive findings.
negative_controls: Test for effect modification by low weight on outcomes not plausibly affected by alteplase (e.g., incidence of unrelated chronic conditions recorded at 6 months) as a falsification check, if available.
Examine treatment*weight interaction on early biomarkers unlikely to be causally downstream of alteplase (e.g., baseline laboratory values) to detect spurious associations.
robustness: Repeat primary interaction using alternative estimators (GLM, TMLE, IPTW) and report consistency.
Sensitivity analysis for unmeasured confounding of the interaction: compute E-values for the observed interaction estimate and for subgroup-specific effects.
Bootstrap or permutation tests for the interaction to account for small-sample distributional issues.
Pre-specify minimum subgroup event count threshold (e.g., ≥10 events per arm) and treat any result below threshold as exploratory.

caveats: Randomization in IST-3 pertains to treatment, not subgroup membership: while treatment effect estimates are unbiased overall, subgroup interaction tests are observational comparisons and are less reliable—any interaction should be considered hypothesis-generating and require replication.
Small total sample (N≈200) limits precision: expect wide CIs and limited power to detect realistic interaction sizes; null findings do not rule out clinically important effect modification.

Threshold choice and sex imbalance: The absolute 60 kg cut-point may disproportionately select women; use sensitivity analyses with BMI and sex-specific thresholds before attributing effects to weight per se.
Mediation assumptions are strong: Estimating the fraction mediated by sICH requires no unmeasured mediator–outcome confounding and correct model specification; interpret mediation results cautiously.
Measurement and missing data: Imputation and analytic choices for missing weight or covariates can materially affect results—report analyses by measured-only and imputed datasets.

Multiplicity and selective reporting: Multiple subgroup/threshold tests inflate false positive risk. Any positive interaction should be validated in independent datasets or prespecified meta-analytic subgroup assessments before clinical action.

hypotheses.title: Moderate body weight (60-99 kg) modifies benefit from IV alteplase for acute ischemic stroke
hypotheses.hypothesis: Among acute ischemic stroke patients treated within 6 hours, those with body weight in the moderate range (60-99 kg) derive greater benefit from IV alteplase (rtPA) on the outcome Alive and independent (OHS 0-2) at 6 months than low-weight (<60 kg) or very-high-weight (>=100 kg) patients.

subgroup.split_rule: weight >= 60 kg and weight <= 99 kg (categorical: <60 kg, 60-99 kg, >=100 kg)
subgroup.notes: Weight measured at baseline (admission). Use recorded weight; if only estimated weight available, flag and run sensitivity. Rationale assumes standard dosing (0.9 mg/kg up to 90 mg cap). For patients >=100 kg the per-kg dose is effectively reduced by the 90 mg cap; for <60 kg increased frailty/comorbidity may reduce net benefit.

rationale: Pharmacologic dosing rationale: Alteplase is administered by weight (0.9 mg/kg) with a common protocol maximum (90 mg). Patients 60-99 kg receive near-target per-kg exposure without encountering the dose cap; those >=100 kg receive a capped dose resulting in lower mg/kg exposure that could reduce recanalization efficacy.

Bleeding vs efficacy balance: Very low-weight patients may have higher relative bleeding risk or greater frailty and comorbidity burden that limits recovery, while mid-weight patients may have an optimal balance between sufficient fibrinolytic exposure and acceptable hemorrhagic risk.

Clinical plausibility and prior literature: Observational and pharmacokinetic analyses in thrombolysis/antithrombotic therapy suggest non-linear relationships between body size and treatment effect, with extremes of weight often showing attenuated benefit or higher harm; analogous patterns have been reported for dose-capped agents.

Mechanistic link to outcomes: Greater effective per-kg dosing in the 60-99 kg band plausibly increases probability of successful reperfusion (improving functional outcome) without a proportionate rise in symptomatic intracerebral hemorrhage compared with extremes.

Operational/practical considerations: Weight extremes correlate with other effect modifiers (frailty, comorbidity, care decisions) that can alter observed treatment benefit, making the mid-weight group more likely to realize intended pharmacologic benefit.
key_features: Baseline body weight (kg)
Dose per kg received and presence of dose-capping (absolute alteplase dose, capped vs uncapped)
Frailty and comorbidity markers (age, pre-stroke mRS, Charlson comorbidity components)
Stroke severity (baseline NIHSS)
Time-to-treatment (onset-to-needle)
confounders_and_bias_risks: Confounding by indication/selection: clinicians may treat or withhold treatment differently by weight (or by related factors such as obesity-related comorbidities), producing non-random distribution of prognostic factors across weight strata.

Measured confounding: weight correlates with age, sex, baseline NIHSS, pre-stroke disability, diabetes, atrial fibrillation, hypertension — insufficient adjustment can produce spurious subgroup differences.
Collider bias: conditioning on variables that are downstream of both weight and outcome (for example early complications or treatment modifications) can induce artificial associations.
Measurement error in weight: estimated vs measured weight in the acute setting can misclassify subgroup membership, biasing interactions toward the null or creating artifacts.

Dose-capping is protocol-driven: the cap (e.g., 90 mg) produces a mechanical per-kg exposure difference for >=100 kg patients — observed differences could reflect dose rather than inherent weight biology.
Small sample / multiple testing: with n=200 and multiple subgroup comparisons, estimates will be imprecise and susceptible to random variation and type I error.

analyses: Primary test: fit an adjusted regression model for outcome (Alive and independent at 6 months) including treatment, categorical weight group (<60, 60-99, >=100), and a treatment*weight_group interaction term; report interaction p-value and subgroup-specific average treatment effects (risk difference and risk ratio) with 95% CIs.

Doubly-robust estimation: estimate subgroup-specific treatment effects using doubly-robust methods (e.g., inverse-probability weighting + outcome regression or targeted maximum likelihood estimation) adjusting for key confounders (age, baseline NIHSS, onset-to-needle time, sex, pre-stroke mRS, diabetes, atrial fibrillation, systolic BP, glucose, center).

Continuous-weight analysis: model weight continuously with restricted cubic splines and include a treatment*spline interaction to assess non-linearity and identify range of maximal benefit (plot marginal treatment effect vs weight with confidence bands).

Dose mediation check: calculate actual mg/kg dose or percent-of-target dose and test mediation (or stratify) to assess whether reduced per-kg dosing in >=100 kg explains any attenuation of benefit (mediation analysis or interaction of treatment with dose-per-kg).

Sensitivity analyses: multiple imputation for missing covariates/outcomes, exclude cases with estimated (not measured) weight, and repeat analysis restricting to patients without major protocol deviations.

Secondary/endpoints: repeat analyses for related outcomes (6-month mortality, symptomatic intracerebral hemorrhage by standard definitions, ordinal shift in OHS) to check consistency of direction and magnitude.

Unmeasured confounding assessment: compute E-values for observed subgroup-specific risk differences and perform quantitative bias analysis to gauge strength of an unmeasured confounder necessary to explain the interaction.
Resampling/stability: bootstrap confidence intervals and repeat subgroup discovery on resamples to assess stability of the identified weight range given modest sample size.
negative_controls: Analyze an outcome unlikely to be affected by alteplase (e.g., non-stroke-related in-hospital infections or fractures) for spurious associations with treatment*weight interaction.
Test interaction between treatment and a baseline variable unrelated to pharmacology (e.g., left vs right-sided dominance if available) as a falsification check.
robustness: Repeat analyses using different weight cutpoints (e.g., 55-74 / 75-94 / >=95) to ensure findings are not an artifact of chosen bins.
Adjust additionally for BMI and height where available to see whether body composition (rather than absolute weight) explains effects.
Per-protocol vs intention-to-treat comparison if treatment compliance/misclassification exists.
Assess influence of individual centers (fixed effects or leave-one-center-out) to rule out center-level confounding.

caveats: Subgroup findings do not establish causality: even within randomized trials, treatment-by-subgroup interactions are observational contrasts and can be confounded; a significant interaction must be interpreted cautiously.
Small effective sample size and multiple comparisons increase the chance of false positives and imprecise effect estimates; emphasize effect sizes and CIs rather than P-values alone.

Observed effect modification may reflect dosing differences (protocol cap) rather than intrinsic biologic differences by weight; mediation analysis is required before attributing benefit to weight per se.
Weight is correlated with sex, height, and comorbidity; residual confounding may remain despite adjustment — especially frailty and socio-demographic factors not fully captured in the dataset.

Measurement issues (estimated vs measured weight) and differences in clinical care by weight strata can bias results; replication in larger datasets or pooled trials is needed before making clinical recommendations.

hypotheses.title: Marked admission hyperglycaemia (glucose >= 10 mmol/L) attenuates benefit of IV alteplase
hypotheses.hypothesis: Among acute ischemic stroke patients treated within 6 hours, those with admission blood glucose >= 10 mmol/L have a lower probability of being alive and independent (OHS 0-2) at 6 months after IV alteplase than patients with lower glucose, and the relative and absolute benefit of alteplase versus control is smaller in the glucose >= 10 mmol/L subgroup (effect modification by admission hyperglycaemia).

subgroup.split_rule: Admission blood glucose >= 10.0 mmol/L versus < 10.0 mmol/L
subgroup.notes: Use first (admission) venous plasma glucose measurement where available; if only capillary reported, convert/annotate. If multiple baseline measurements exist use the earliest taken prior to any glucose-lowering treatment. Missing baseline glucose should be imputed cautiously (see validation plan). Consider alternative encodings (continuous, splines, other cutpoints 7, 8, 11 mmol/L) in sensitivity analyses.

rationale: Pathophysiology: Acute hyperglycaemia during cerebral ischemia increases anaerobic glycolysis and lactic acid production in ischemic tissue, promoting infarct growth and reducing salvageable penumbra — mechanisms that plausibly reduce the net benefit of reperfusion therapies.

Haemorrhagic transformation risk: Hyperglycaemia exacerbates blood–brain barrier disruption and oxidative stress in reperfused tissue in preclinical models, increasing risk of haemorrhagic transformation after reperfusion and thereby potentially blunting functional gains from thrombolysis.

Observational clinical evidence: Multiple observational cohorts report associations between higher admission glucose and larger infarct volumes, increased symptomatic intracerebral haemorrhage (sICH) after thrombolysis, and worse 3–6 month functional outcomes, consistent with an interaction where hyperglycaemia worsens outcome even after reperfusion.

Therapeutic implication and guideline relevance: Because hyperglycaemia is modifiable acutely and some clinical guidance recommends correction, it is clinically relevant to know whether marked hyperglycaemia modifies the randomized alteplase effect size (i.e., whether benefit is reduced enough to affect treatment decisions).

Distinguishing acute stress from chronic glycaemic state: Acute admission glucose may reflect stress hyperglycaemia (poor prognostic sign) or poorly controlled diabetes; both biological pathways plausibly interact with reperfusion but may differ in magnitude — so investigation should adjust for diabetes history or HbA1c when available.
key_features: Admission blood glucose (mmol/L)
Treatment allocation (IV alteplase vs control; randomized in IST-3)
Baseline stroke severity (NIHSS)
Time from symptom onset to randomization/needle (onset-to-treatment time)
Diabetes history / HbA1c (if available) and acute glucose-lowering therapy given
confounders_and_bias_risks: Prognostic confounding by stroke severity: higher admission glucose is associated with greater stroke severity (higher NIHSS) and larger infarcts; if not fully adjusted, apparent modification may reflect residual prognostic differences rather than true interaction.
Chronic vs acute hyperglycaemia: without HbA1c, elevated glucose may represent chronic diabetes or acute stress hyperglycaemia; these have different implications and different confounding structures.

Measurement error and timing: variability in glucose assay type (capillary vs plasma), timing relative to onset or pre-hospital glucose-lowering therapy, and missing values can bias subgroup assignment and attenuate or exaggerate interaction estimates.

Collider selection bias if restricting to treated patients only: analyzing only alteplase recipients breaks randomization; interaction tests should compare randomized arms within glucose strata to preserve causal inference.

Small sample and low event counts: with total n≈200 and a likely small subgroup of glucose >=10, interaction tests will have low power and wide CIs; chance findings and regression-to-the-mean are possible.
Residual confounding by treatment delays, blood pressure, prior disability, stroke subtype (large vessel occlusion), and concomitant treatments not fully accounted for.

analyses: Primary analysis: estimate the randomized treatment effect (alteplase vs control) on OHS 0-2 at 6 months within glucose strata (<10 and >=10 mmol/L). Report absolute risk differences and risk ratios with 95% CIs. Use intention-to-treat principle to preserve randomization.

Interaction test: fit a multivariable logistic regression for OHS 0-2 including terms for treatment, glucose subgroup indicator, and a treatment*glucose interaction; adjust for pre-specified baseline covariates (age, baseline NIHSS, time-to-treatment, baseline mRS, diabetes history, SBP, atrial fibrillation, imaging-confirmed large-vessel occlusion if available). Report p-value and interaction effect estimate (ratio of odds ratios or difference in risk differences).

Continuous and flexible modeling: model baseline glucose continuously with restricted cubic splines and include interaction terms between continuous glucose and treatment to explore nonlinear effect modification and to avoid arbitrary dichotomization.

Doubly-robust / causal estimators: estimate conditional average treatment effects using IPTW or targeted maximum likelihood estimation (TMLE) stratified by glucose subgroup to reduce model dependence; present adjusted absolute treatment effects with bootstrap CIs.

Sensitivity analyses: (a) exclude known diabetics and repeat interaction tests to probe acute stress hyperglycaemia; (b) adjust for HbA1c (if available) to separate chronic glycaemic control; (c) vary glucose threshold (>=7, >=8, >=11 mmol/L) and present patterns across thresholds; (d) assess robustness to missing glucose via multiple imputation with chained equations including outcome predictors.

Safety/outcome mediation checks: compare rates of symptomatic intracerebral haemorrhage and early infarct growth between glucose strata and treatment arms to assess whether increased harm mediates reduced benefit.

Negative control/falsification: test for interaction between treatment and a baseline variable unlikely to modify thrombolysis effect (e.g., baseline serum sodium within normal range) to check for spurious interaction signals.
Estimate statistical power: report post-hoc detectable interaction size given subgroup sample sizes and event rates; interpret null interaction accordingly.
